units.spoken: RLHF with PPO (InstructGPT)
The three-stage recipe that taught a large language model to follow instructions.
This page builds on RL Basics and Aligning Language Models with RL. The terms below are the ones this page keeps using.

An agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.
A token is a word or a piece of a word; a language model writes its reply one token at a time.

Here the agent is the language model. Here the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, and the move is the next token. Here the reward is one number for the whole reply, given when the reply ends.
RL, short for reinforcement learning, is learning which moves to make from rewards rather than from labeled answers.
A policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The policy is the language model being trained to write replies.

sections.section: 1 Why a score is not enough

units.spoken: Section one, Why a score is not enough
A score alone changes nothing
What. Picture a tutor who grades essays but never changes how she teaches. A score alone is that tutor: it can rank any reply, but it cannot teach the model to write a better one.
How. Something must turn the scores into training, pushing the model toward replies that score high.
Why. When it works, the model writes replies the labelers prefer, not just replies it can score.
Three stages, one recipe
What. Picture three handoffs in a row. The labelers write good replies, the labelers compare replies, and the model learns from both.
How. Demonstrations train the first stage, comparisons train the reward model, and the reward model's scores train the policy by reinforcement learning.
Why. When it works, each stage hands the next one exactly what it needs: examples to copy, a scorer that matches the labelers' picks, and a policy that chases the scorer.
A network trained to score replies the way the labelers would can score any reply; something must train the language model to write replies that score high.
The running example is a prompt, "Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old", with replies such as a simple story or a list of dates, and a person saying which reply is better.

Take a look at this figure. One prompt, two replies: the simple story and the list of dates. The person marks the story better, and that mark is the label the reward model learns from. The lesson is that RLHF starts from a person's pick, not from a score.

Figure 1 shows where RLHF starts: the person's pick is the label the reward model learns from: the simple story is marked better than the list of dates, so the pair teaches the scorer that this kind of reply should score higher.

InstructGPT trained GPT-3, a large pretrained language model, to follow instructions. The labelers, the people OpenAI hired, wrote replies and compared them for prompts sent to OpenAI's service. The reward model learns their stated preferences, not people's in general.
A reward model is a language model with a one-number output, trained on the labelers' comparisons so the reply they preferred scores higher.

Take a look at this figure. Three stages in a chain: supervised fine-tuning copies the demonstrations, the reward model learns to score the way the labelers would, and reinforcement learning trains the policy toward the story's score. The lesson is the order: people feed the first two stages, and the loop trains last.

Figure 2 shows the three stages as a chain that turns human judgment into training: supervised fine-tuning copies the demonstrations, the reward model learns to score the way the labelers would, and reinforcement learning trains the policy toward the story's score. Take the moon-landing prompt: the story is first a demonstration to copy, then the preferred half of a comparison, then the reply whose score the policy chases.
RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, is that three-stage recipe.

The labelers' work enters twice: once as written replies and once as comparisons. Replies the labelers write to show the wanted behavior are called demonstrations. The first stage, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), trains on them with the ordinary next-token loss, which teaches the model to predict each next token. SFT copies demonstrations but cannot learn from "this is better than that".

sections.section: 2 One score per reply, small steps toward it

units.spoken: Section two, One score per reply, small steps toward it
One score, split across tokens
What. Picture the story earning one number at the end, after its last token. Every token shares that one score, and the method must work out which tokens earned it.
How. The policy starts as the SFT model, writes replies, and takes small, limited steps toward higher scores, with each token pushed by its own share of the score.
Why. When it works, the tokens that made the story good get pushed up, and the ones that did not get pushed down, even though only the whole reply was scored.

Take a look at this figure. Five tokens, one score: the score sits after the last token, with an arrow back to "astronauts". The lesson is that the score arrives only when the reply is finished, so no single token is told it earned it.
Figure 3 draws the score as one box after the five tokens, with an arrow back to "astronauts": the score arrives only when the reply is finished.
Nobody tells the model which words to change; it only sees each reply's score.

In RLHF the scores come from the reward model trained in the second stage. The policy starts as the SFT model, so at first it writes replies like the ones the labelers demonstrated. An episode is one run from the start until it ends. Here one episode is one reply. The third stage repeats this over many prompts.

The reference model is a frozen copy of the SFT model. KL measures how different two probability distributions are, zero when they match; the KL penalty charges the policy for drifting away from the reference model. The reward is the reward model's score at the end minus a KL penalty, and an RL update that takes small, limited steps trains the policy to earn it.
2.1 From demonstrations to reinforcement learning
The critic guesses the return
What. Picture a second network watching each partial reply and guessing how it will end. That guess is what lets the method credit individual tokens.
How. The critic starts as a copy of the reward model, initialized from it, and learns to guess the return, all the reward still to come, for each partial reply.
Why. When it works, each token is pushed by how much better it did than the critic guessed, so the credit lands on the tokens that earned it.
The second and third stages can repeat on fresh comparisons once the policy has moved on.
The critic learns to guess the return of each partial reply of the story.

sections.section: 3 The objective and the reward per token

units.spoken: Section three, The objective and the reward per token

The goal is the score the policy gets on average, not on one lucky reply. An expected value is that average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is. The prompts the model is trained on form one training set. One prompt can get many different replies, and the policy might write any of them. So Equation 1 scores the replies the policy actually writes, on the prompts it is trained on.
Ordinary pretraining text comes from the model's original pretraining set. Mixing such text back in keeps the model good at ordinary writing.
Equation 1. The InstructGPT objective. The objective is the average score of the replies the policy writes, minus the price of drifting from the reference.
Take a look at this equation. The objective is the average score of the replies the policy writes, minus the price of drifting from the reference.

The objective line. J sub R L H F of thay-ta is the objective, a number scoring how well the policy does. Thay-ta is the policy's weights, the numbers training changes. E is the average over everything that can happen by chance. Ex is one prompt, drawn from the training set. Dee is the training set, the prompts the model trains on. Why is one reply the policy writes to that prompt. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy itself, giving each reply its chance. The big bracket holds the per-reply payoff, the score minus the price of drifting. Intuitively, the objective is the average payoff over every prompt and every reply the policy might write.
termList: J sub R L H F of thay-ta

units.spoken: Intuition. The objective is an average over everything the policy might do: every prompt, every reply.
Example. Take the moon-landing prompt: the average runs over every reply the policy might write to it, each weighed by its chance.

The payoff line. Ar sub sigh of ex and why is the reward model's score for this reply to this prompt. Beta is the KL penalty strength, setting how hard the penalty bites. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy's chance of this reply given this prompt. Pee sub ref is the reference's chance of the same reply. The log ratio compares the two chances: zero when they match, positive when the policy likes the reply more. The minus subtracts the penalty from the score. Intuitively, the payoff is the score minus beta times the drift, so drifting from the reference costs.
Intuition. The payoff is the score minus the price of drifting.
Example. Take the story the policy writes: its score is the reward, and the penalty charges it for liking the story more than the reference does.

The pretraining line. Lambda sub pee tee ex is the pretraining weight, trading a little reward for ordinary writing. E is again an average, this time over pretraining text. Ex sub pree is one piece of ordinary pretraining text. Dee sub pree is the model's original pretraining set. The plus adds this term to the objective. Intuitively, the pretraining term rewards the policy for predicting ordinary text well, so ordinary writing stays good.
Intuition. A second term keeps the model good at ordinary writing.
Example. Take a piece of ordinary text: the pretraining term rewards the policy for predicting it well, so ordinary writing stays good while the policy chases reward.

The log-chance line. Log of pee sub thay-ta of ex sub pree is the log of the policy's chance of the pretraining text. The log turns a chance into a score that grows as the policy predicts better. Intuitively, the last line is the log-chance of the pretraining text itself, and the small bracket closes the pretraining term.
Intuition. The last line is the log-chance of the pretraining text itself.
Example. Take a piece of ordinary text the policy predicts well: its log-chance is high, so the pretraining term rewards it.
So the objective is the average score of the replies the policy writes, minus the price of drifting, plus a pretraining term that keeps ordinary writing good.

Take the moon-landing prompt and the simple story the policy writes for it. The reward model scores the story, the KL penalty charges the policy for liking the story more than the frozen reference does, and a piece of ordinary pretraining text keeps the model good at plain writing, so training pushes the story's score up while holding the policy close to where it started.

The paper writes the policy as pee are ell sub fee, the reference as pee ess eff tee, the reward model as ar sub thay-ta, the pretraining weight as gamma, and the pretraining text as ex; this page writes pee sub thay-ta, pee sub ref, ar sub sigh, lambda sub pee tee ex, and ex sub pree, and keeps its own letters.

So the objective trades reward against drift, and can mix in ordinary text. PPO, proximal policy optimization, is the RL method the walkthrough below uses to update the policy. Setting lambda sub pee tee ex above zero gives PPO-ptx. InstructGPT's final models use it, so every RL update also sees a batch of pretraining text.

The alignment tax is the drop in ordinary benchmark scores an aligned model can suffer. Lines 3 and 4 are there to shrink that tax: they trade a little reward for keeping the model's ordinary writing skills. In RL Basics, the reward after a move is named by the step it follows; here the move is one token of the reply, so the reward after token tee is ar sub tee plus one. The example follows the story's first five tokens, ending at astronauts. So the reward after each token is a small KL penalty, and the reward model's score arrives once, after the last token.

Equation 2. The reward per token. One score at the end of a reply cannot say which token earned it, so the reward has to be split across tokens. A coach who only sees the final score of a game faces the same problem: the praise has to reach the plays that earned it.
Take a look at this equation. Each token pays its own small penalty, and only the last token brings the reply's score.

The token reward line. Ar sub tee plus one is the reward following token tee, where tee is its position in the reply. Why sub tee is the token itself. Why sub less than tee is the tokens already written before it. Beta is the KL penalty strength, the weight that prices drift. Pee sub thay-ta is the policy's chance of this token given the prompt and the tokens before it. Pee sub ref is the reference's chance of the same token. The log ratio is zero at a match, and the minus turns it into a penalty. Intuitively, each token pays its own small penalty for drifting from the reference.
Intuition. Each token pays its own small penalty.
Example. Take the token "time": its reward is the penalty for liking it more than the reference does.

The last-token line. The marker one bracket tee equals capital tee is one only when this token is the last one. Tee is the token's position, and capital tee is the last position. Ar sub sigh of ex and why is the reward model's score for the whole finished reply. The plus adds the score to the token's penalty, but only for the last token. Intuitively, only the last token brings the score, so the score lands once, on "astronauts".
termList: one bracket tee equals capital tee

units.spoken: Intuition. Only the last token brings the score.
Example. Take the finished story: the reward model reads all five tokens at once and hands its one score to "astronauts", the last token, to carry.
So each token's reward is its own small KL penalty, and only the last token brings the reply's score.
Take the story's five tokens together: the two lines set the reward after each one, so the walkthrough can push each token by how well it turned out.
Most RLHF code writes this reward as ar sub tee; it is the same reward, indexed by the token it follows.
This is the reward stream the walkthrough's RL update works on.

sections.section: 4 One RL step on a batch of replies

units.spoken: Section four, One RL step on a batch of replies
4.1 One PPO update on the story’s tokens

The policy gradient pushes each move the agent played up or down by how well it turned out. Here the score of each token is built in the walkthrough's steps from the real rewards and the critic's guess. Here a batch is a set of prompts and the replies the policy just wrote for them, trained on together. So the tokens of one reply can be pushed by different amounts, even though the reply earned one score.

PPO is the policy-gradient method that makes small, limited updates so one batch cannot wreck the policy. One PPO step in RLHF uses four networks: the policy, the reference model, the reward model and the critic.
One RL step: the policy writes replies, the reward model scores them, and PPO updates the policy.

Take a look at this walkthrough. It runs one PPO update on a batch of three prompts, the moon-landing prompt among them. The policy writes a reply to each, the reference reads the same tokens, and the reward model scores each finished reply. Each token pays a small KL penalty, the critic guesses each partial reply's value, and the advantage pushes tokens up or down. The ratio is clipped so one update cannot move a token far, and pretraining text keeps ordinary writing good.

Try the walkthrough. Press Play to run one PPO update on the batch, or step through it with Next. Watch the policy write its replies, the reference read them, the reward model score them, and each token pay its KL penalty; then watch the critic guess, the advantage push tokens up, the ratio clip, and the pretraining text feed in. Press Reset to start over.
The walkthrough runs one PPO update on the batch the policy just wrote, token by token.
Take a look at this walkthrough. It runs one PPO update on the batch the policy just wrote, token by token, and the score lands on the last token of the story.

The scoring step. The walkthrough reaches the scoring step. Each reply earns its score minus its drift, and the check at the end of the story's reply marks its score. The line turns that score into the payoff by subtracting the price of drifting from the reference.
Intuition. The walkthrough reaches the scoring step: each reply earns its score minus its drift.
Example. Take the story's check at the end of its reply: it marks the score, and the line turns that score into the payoff by subtracting the price of drifting from the reference.

The penalty step. The walkthrough follows the penalty token by token. A small brown bar sits under each token of the story, marking the penalty for liking that token more than the reference does. The score joins only at the last token.
Intuition. The walkthrough follows the penalty token by token.
Example. Take the token "time": a small brown bar sits under it, marking the penalty for liking "time" more than the reference does.

The last-token step. The walkthrough reaches the last token. "Astronauts" brings the reward model's score on top of its penalty, while earlier tokens pay only their penalty. The score lands once, at the end of the story.
Intuition. The walkthrough reaches the last token.
Example. Take the finished story: the reward model reads all five tokens at once and hands its one score to "astronauts", the last token, to carry.

The pretraining step. The walkthrough adds pretraining text beside the RL update. A side box feeds the pretraining gradient in with the RL gradient, so the same step that chases reward also keeps ordinary writing good.
Intuition. The walkthrough adds pretraining text beside the RL update.
Example. Take the side box beside the update: it feeds the pretraining gradient in with the RL gradient, so the same step that chases reward also keeps ordinary writing good.
The log-chance step. The walkthrough's last line is the pretraining log-chance. It rewards the policy for predicting ordinary text well, and the small bracket closes the pretraining term.
Intuition. The walkthrough's last line is the pretraining log-chance.
Example. The pretraining text's log-chance rewards the policy for predicting ordinary text well.

Summary. Take one RL step on a batch holding the moon-landing prompt. The policy's simple story earns its score minus its KL drift, each of its tokens pays a small penalty with the score landing on "astronauts", and a batch of pretraining text keeps ordinary writing good, so PPO pushes each token by how well it turned out.
4.2 Which models train and which stay frozen

The policy writes the story, the reference reads the same story tokens, the reward model scores the finished story, and the critic guesses each partial story's value. The policy, the reference model and the critic run on every token, while the reward model runs once per reply. The loop repeats for 256k episodes.

Take a look at this figure. Four models around one story: the policy writes it, the reference reads it, the reward model scores it, and the critic guesses each partial reply's value. The policy and the critic learn; the reference and the reward model hold still. The lesson is the split: the two that learn move, and the two that anchor stay frozen.

Figure 4 shows the split: the frozen models are the anchors, the reference reading the same story the policy writes so the KL penalty can be measured, and the reward model scoring the finished story without moving. Take the moon-landing prompt: the policy writes the story, the critic guesses each partial reply's value, and the two frozen models hold still while the other two learn.

sections.section: 5 Rewards per token and the PPO-ptx loss

units.spoken: Section five, Rewards per token and the PPO-ptx loss

pee pee oh loss is the clipped PPO loss from Proximal Policy Optimization, computed with advantages from these rewards, where a token's advantage is how much better it did than the critic guessed. The clipped objective takes the smaller of the unclipped ratio times the advantage and the clipped ratio times the advantage, so an update stops rewarding a helpful change once it passes an edge; the formula is on the PPO page. Inputs are per-token log-probs, the log of each token's probability. Column tee of ar holds ar sub tee plus one, the reward after token tee. The per-token rewards are computed without gradients, because they are targets for PPO, not something to backpropagate through.
The code below turns the story reply's tokens into per-token rewards: a small KL penalty after each token, the reward model's score after the last one.

This code turns the story's tokens into per-token rewards and builds the PPO-ptx loss. The first function takes the policy's and the reference's log-chances for each token: each token's reward is minus beta times the gap between them, and the last token gets the reward model's score added on top. The second function adds the pretraining loss, weighted by lambda sub pee tee ex, to the clipped PPO loss. The rewards are computed without gradients, because they are targets, not something to backpropagate through.
1. The per-token reward card: a KL penalty after every token, the reward model's score after the last one.
2. Lines 3 and 4 of the InstructGPT objective card: the PPO loss plus the pretraining loss, weighted.

sections.section: 6 How the KL penalty holds the policy back

units.spoken: Section six, How the KL penalty holds the policy back
A price on drifting from the reference

What. Picture the policy as a reply writer who wants the highest score and a reference model standing beside it, holding the original writing. The best policy is the one that earns the highest score minus the price of drifting from the reference.
How. Beta sets the price: a high beta keeps the policy close to the reference, a low beta lets it chase the reward.
Why. When it works, the policy moves just far enough to earn more reward without drifting into replies the reward model over-scores.
The tool shows five replies: the simple story and the list of dates from Figure 1, a story with a joke, a refusal, and the padded story.

The padded flattering story is the reply the reward model over-scores: long and flattering, it can win when the penalty is weak. It is an illustrative reply made for this tool, not a reported InstructGPT observation.

Take a look at this figure. Five replies, each with two bars: the grey bar is the reference, the teal bar the policy after the penalty. The padded story is the one the reward model over-scores. The lesson is that the penalty holds the policy's bars close to the reference's, and a weak penalty lets the padded story's bar run past the rest.

Try the tool. Drag the penalty slider toward chasing the reward and watch the teal bars stretch away from the grey ones; drag it back toward staying close and they pull in. Flip the toggle to give the padded story its bonus, and watch it become the most likely reply at a weak penalty.
The KL penalty strength decides how far the policy moves from the reference toward what the reward model likes.

The tool shows how the KL penalty holds the policy back: the grey bar is the reference, the teal bar the policy after the penalty. The slider sets the penalty strength: dragging it toward chasing the reward stretches the teal bars away from the grey ones, while dragging it toward staying close pulls them back. Take the simple story: with the toggle off, it stays the most likely reply at every point the slider was tried.

Take a look at this figure. The reward model now over-scores long, padded-out replies. At a weak penalty the padded story's teal bar lifts past its grey bar and past the simple story's teal bar, so the padded story becomes the most likely reply. The lesson is that when the reward model over-scores length, a weak penalty lets the padded story win.

Figure 5 flips the reward model to one that over-scores long, padded-out replies, and at a weak penalty the padded story becomes the most likely reply. With the toggle on at a weak penalty, the bonus lifts the padded story's teal bar past its grey bar and past the simple story's teal bar, and the gauge of distance from the reference grows.
Section seven, Running RLHF in practice

These are the settings that trained the model to write replies like the moon-landing pair: the KL penalty that holds the story close to the reference, and the pretraining weight that keeps ordinary text good.

The settings trade training effort against drift: more episodes or a lower KL penalty let the policy chase reward further, while a higher penalty or more pretraining weight holds it closer to where it started. Take the KL penalty strength: raising it keeps the policy near the SFT model with less hacking, while lowering it lets the policy chase reward and drift.

This table lines up the six settings that trained InstructGPT, with what raising and lowering each one does. Read across a row to see one setting's trade-off, and down the Raise and Lower columns to compare. The KL penalty strength beta is 0.02: raising it keeps the policy near the SFT model with less hacking, while lowering it lets the policy chase reward, drift, and hack. The pretraining weight lambda sub pee tee ex is 27.8: raising it means less alignment tax but slower reward gain, while lowering it means more tax. Episodes in the RL stage are 256k, from about 31k distinct prompts: more episodes mean more training but more drift risk, fewer mean less training. Replies per batch are 512: more mean steadier updates and more memory, fewer mean noisier updates. PPO runs 1 epoch with minibatches of 64: reusing each batch more risks drift, reusing it less means less reuse. The PPO clip is 0.2: a bigger clip means bigger steps, a smaller clip means smaller steps. The pattern is that every setting trades training effort against drift: more training or a weaker penalty chases reward further, while a stronger penalty or more pretraining weight holds the policy closer to where it started.
TRL, Hugging Face's open library for training language models with these methods, has a PPO trainer; watch the logged KL, which should rise slowly, not jump.
The run behind those settings used prompts sent to the OpenAI API plus prompts the labelers wrote. The policy that RL starts from is a separate SFT run with some pretraining text mixed in.

The paper counts the 175B PPO-ptx run at 60 petaflops/s-days of compute, the total arithmetic of the run, against 4.9 for the 175B SFT model, so the RL stage costs about twelve times the supervised stage before it. The run also holds four models at once: the 175B policy, its frozen 175B reference copy, the 6B reward model and the 6B critic, 362 billion parameters in all, about 724 GB of weights alone.

sections.section: 8 When RLHF with PPO is worth its cost

units.spoken: Section eight, When RLHF with PPO is worth its cost
Only when no right answer can be copied
What. Picture a reply you can only judge once it is written, with no right answer to copy. That is when RLHF earns its cost.
How. RLHF is on-policy: it learns only from replies the current policy just wrote, exploring fresh replies and keeping the ones that score high.
Why. When it works, the model finds better replies than any demonstration showed.
The labelers preferred the 175B InstructGPT replies to the 175B GPT-3 replies 85 times out of 100, which is what the twelvefold cost buys.
Section nine, How RLHF goes wrong
The fixes in Table 2 draw on later methods and model sizes.
Reward hacking is when the policy finds replies that score high without being good.
GRPO, group relative policy optimization, scores a group of replies to one prompt against each other and uses the group's average as the bar.
In InstructGPT the critic is far smaller than the policy, because it starts from the 6B reward model while the policy is 175B.
Constitutional AI is a later method in which a model guided by a written list of principles writes the harm labels that mark a reply as harmful.

Each failure has a visible symptom and a concrete fix: when the KL penalty climbs and the padded story wins, the penalty is too weak, and the fix is to raise beta or stop early. Take reward hacking: when the reward climbs for the padded story while human ratings fall, the fix is to stop early and retrain the reward model on new replies.

This table lines up six ways RLHF goes wrong, what each one looks like, and what fixes it. Read across a row to see one failure's symptom and fix, and down the rows to compare the failures. When beta is too low, the KL climbs and the padded flattering story wins; the fix is to raise beta or stop early. When beta is too high, nothing changes from SFT; the fix is to lower beta. Reward hacking is when the reward climbs for the padded story while human ratings fall; the fix is to stop early and retrain the reward model on new replies. The alignment tax is when scores on standard language benchmarks drop after RL; the fix is PPO-ptx. The critic and the reward model cost memory for four models, and a 175B reward model trains unstably; the fix is a 6B reward model and a smaller critic, or removing the critic as GRPO does. When helpfulness labels reward compliance, a harmful request, such as how to break into a neighbor's wifi, gets answered helpfully; the fix is separate harmlessness data, as in Constitutional AI. The pattern is that most failures are the penalty too weak or too strong, or the reward model fooled, and each has a concrete fix.

sections.section: 10 What later methods swap or drop in this pipeline

units.spoken: Section ten, What later methods swap or drop in this pipeline
Each later method changes one box of this pipeline.

Constitutional AI and RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, replace the human labeler who picked the story with an AI labeler. GRPO drops the critic that guessed the story's value. DPO, direct preference optimization, drops the reward model and the RL step itself.
Can an AI write the harm labels instead of the labelers? Constitutional AI, the next page, answers it.
